Over the past five months, the Japanese government and several Japanese universities have launched significant new initiatives to increase funding and resources to attract and support scholars impacted by funding cuts in the United States, particularly those resulting from the policies of the Trump administration.

Key developments include:

Government Funding Initiatives:

In June 2025, the Japanese government announced the “J-RISE Initiative” (Japan Research & Innovation for Scientific Excellence), a strategic program with a budget of ¥100 billion (about $693 million) to attract top researchers from abroad, including those affected by US funding reductions
. This initiative is designed to make Japan a more attractive destination for global scientific talent by improving salaries, research environments, and support systems
.

The initiative leverages the revenue from Japan’s 10 trillion yen University Fund, with a portion earmarked for urgent measures to recruit both foreign and overseas Japanese researchers
. The Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology (MEXT) has allocated ¥3.3 billion (about $23 million) over three years to subsidize domestic universities accepting foreign researchers, including young researchers and Ph.D. students
.

University-Level Actions:

Osaka University has set aside ¥600 million to ¥1 billion to accept up to 100 US postdoctoral researchers at its Graduate School of Medicine. The university plans to open international applications and provide support for both research and living conditions
.

Tohoku University is investing about ¥30 billion (over $200 million) to recruit approximately 500 researchers from Japan and abroad, with a particular focus on those affected by US funding cuts
.

At least 87 Japanese universities have announced new support measures and budgets to host foreign researchers and students from the US, including tuition waivers, housing support, and acceptance as both regular and non-degree students
. Some universities, such as Tohoku, have conducted recruitment events at major US institutions like Stanford and Harvard
.

Policy and Structural Changes:

The Japanese government is working to address the traditionally lower salaries for researchers compared to the US and Europe, aiming to offer compensation at levels competitive with overseas institutions
.

There are plans to relax certain administrative requirements and improve research infrastructure to make Japan more attractive to international scholars
.

Motivation and Context:
These measures are a direct response to the exodus of researchers from the US, where recent policy changes have led to significant cuts in scientific funding and increased job instability. Japanese officials have explicitly stated that attracting this talent is a national priority, both to enhance Japan’s research capabilities and to compete with similar recruitment drives by Europe and China
.

Summary Table of Major Initiatives

Initiative/University	Funding/Support	Target Group	Key Features
J-RISE Initiative (Govt)	¥100 billion (approx. $693 million)	Top international researchers, incl. US	Salary parity, research environment improvements
MEXT Subsidy Program	¥3.3 billion over 3 years	Young researchers, PhD students	Salaries, research expenses, equipment
Osaka University	¥600 million–¥1 billion	Up to 100 US postdocs	Research, living support, medical sector focus
Tohoku University	¥30 billion (approx. $208 million)	~500 researchers (Japan & abroad)	Recruitment events, family support, infrastructure
87+ Japanese Universities	New budgets, various supports	US/foreign researchers & students	Tuition waivers, housing, flexible admissions
These developments represent a major shift in Japan’s approach to international academic recruitment, with a clear focus on supporting scholars who have been impacted by US funding cuts and creating a more competitive, attractive research environment in Japan
.
